newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG mercenary leader rejects "atrocity" charge.
newsitem.headline: PNG mercenary leader rejects "atrocity" charge.

text.p: A retired British army colonel who led an aborted mercenary operation in Papua New Guinea has rejected an assertion by an Australian academic that his men could have caused an atrocity.

Tim Spicer wrote in a letter to the Australian Institute of International Affairs that soldiers employed by his firm, Sandline International, would have used "minimal force" if they had made an assault against rebels on Bougainville island, 800 km (500 miles) north of Port Moresby.
Spicer's 70 African mercenaries were expelled from PNG in March after an army revolt against the government over its plan to use Sandline to end the nine-year secessionist uprising on the island.
In a speech on April 30, academic James Griffin told the Institute that the assault could have led to "an atrocity of the worst kind".
Griffin, emeritus professor of history at the University of Papua New Guinea, said the Sandline operation would probably have succeeded, but at a terrible cost.
But Spicer said the operation had been carefully planned in order to avoid excessive casualties.

"We would like to point out that the concept of our involvement on Bougainville, and the whole thrust of our training and operational advice for the PNGDF (PNG Defence Force), involved the key principles of minimal force, precision and minimum collateral damage, as well as respect for human rights and the strict adherence to the laws of armed conflict," Spicer wrote.
Griffin told Reuters on Wednesday that he stood by the thrust of his remarks.
"The fallback position of any armies in these positions can lead to unpredictable consequences. The temptation would be there to escalate the conflict," he said.
